analysis.one_liner: Requires a new federal ergonomics rule to protect workers from repetitive-stress injuries.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: referred to a House subcommittee on May 30, 2001, it died there when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ordered the Labor Department to write a new workplace ergonomics standard within two years, protecting workers from work-related back injuries and repetitive-stress injuries. It was a direct response to OSHA's first ergonomics rule — issued in 2000 and repealed by Congress and the President days before this bill was introduced — and it cited a National Academy of Sciences report finding about 1 million lost-work-time injuries a year. The House referred it to committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in repetitive-motion and heavy-lifting jobs — meatpacking, assembly lines, warehouses, nursing homes, and offices — who face the back injuries and repetitive-stress disorders the bill's own findings say knock about 1 million people off the job each year and cost $45–54 billion annually in compensation, lost wages, and lost productivity. A binding standard would have required employers to identify hazards and act before workers get hurt.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers in repetitive-motion and lifting jobs

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Labor to issue a final ergonomics rule within two years of enactment, effective within 90 days — a binding deadline, not an option to study the issue further.

Targets work-related musculoskeletal disorders — the low-back and repetitive-stress injuries the bill's findings say cause roughly 1 million workers to lose work time each year, at an estimated $45–54 billion in annual costs.

Requires the rule to spell out in clear terms when an employer must act, what measures are required, and what the compliance obligations are, plus federally developed training materials and an outreach program to help employers and workers comply before the rule takes effect.
Preserves state workers' compensation laws and leaves OSHA's authority to regulate other workplace hazards untouched, narrowing the bill to its ergonomics purpose.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would have to redesign workstations, adjust job tasks, train staff, and manage injury reporting; the bill itself requires the rule to take account of the cost and feasibility of compliance, an acknowledgment that the burden is real. Some of that cost could pass to consumers as slightly higher prices in affected industries.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on employers: the standard would force job redesign, training, and injury-management programs, and the bill concedes this by instructing the Secretary to weigh the cost and feasibility of compliance before issuing the rule.
Coverage is narrowed: the rule could not apply to disorders a job merely aggravated, so a worker whose existing condition worsens at work would fall outside its protection.

The two-year deadline, backed by 'notwithstanding any other provision of law' language, overrides the normal rulemaking process and puts a complex workplace standard on a fixed clock, which could limit careful tailoring.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and well-documented: injuries that cost roughly 1 million workers lost work time every year would get a binding federal response, not voluntary guidelines. The cost — employer spending on redesign, training, and injury management — is real but was tempered by the bill's own safeguards: clear employer obligations, consideration of cost and feasibility, no preemption of state workers' comp, and government-provided compliance assistance. The main design risk is the rigid statutory deadline for a major rule.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Education and the Workforce Committee on March 27, 2001 and to a subcommittee on May 30, 2001, and never got a hearing or vote before the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: OSHA had issued a workplace ergonomics rule in 2000, cited in the bill at 65 Fed. Reg. 68261, and the bill's title — 'reissuance' — reflected that the rule no longer stood; the bill was introduced on March 27, 2001, days after the repeal of the 2000 rule was signed into law.

The bill would have required the Secretary of Labor to issue a final ergonomics rule within two years, effective within 90 days, covering work-related musculoskeletal disorders and spelling out clear employer obligations.
Its findings put the stakes at about 1 million workers losing time from work each year and $45–54 billion in annual economic burden from these injuries.

Introduced March 27, 2001 with six cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, then to its Subcommittee on Workforce Protections on May 30, 2001 — and the record shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed.
The bill died at the subcommittee when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that would have faced ergonomics-compliance costs: the bill died without a hearing, the 2000 rule stayed repealed, and no federal ergonomics standard protecting these workers was ever issued.

for.name: Rep. Christopher John
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 27, 2001, directing the Labor Secretary to reissue an ergonomics rule.

for.name: 5 of 208 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Reps. Tanner, Cramer, Dooley, Spratt, Carson)

for.name: 1 of 223 House Republicans
for.role: Cosponsor (Rep. Amo Houghton of New York)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — the only Republican support it drew.

for.name: AFL-CIO and workplace-safety advocates
for.what_they_did: Pushed for federal ergonomics protections after the 2000 rule was repealed.

against.name: Rep. John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee of referral, which sent the bill to a subcommittee on May 30, 2001 and never scheduled a hearing or markup.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral March 27, 2001 and sent it to the Workforce Protections Subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or vote followed.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Signed the repeal of OSHA's 2000 ergonomics rule on March 20, 2001, a week before this bill was introduced, setting the posture in which the majority showed no interest in reviving a standard.

against.name: Business groups (U.S. Chamber of Commerce, NFIB and allied employer associations)
against.what_they_did: Opposed the 2000 ergonomics standard and backed its repeal, leaving no appetite in the House majority to take up a reissuance bill.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but thin — five of 208 House Democrats and one of 223 House Republicans — while the Republican-led committee took no action; Congress had repealed the 2000 ergonomics rule on largely party-line votes just a week before this bill was introduced.

industries.industry: Employers with repetitive-motion and heavy-lifting work (meatpacking, manufacturing, warehousing, nursing homes)
industries.note: A mandatory ergonomics rule would require these employers to redesign jobs, add lifting aids and training, and act on hazards before workers are hurt. These employers bore the costs of the 2000 rule, backed its repeal, and its defeat here means they carry no federal ergonomics obligation.

A binding rule creates demand for ergonomic workstations, lifting equipment, and compliance assessments and training. The bill itself directs the government to build outreach and training support, and firms serving that compliance market would grow alongside the safety benefit.
